newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: FOCUS - Manila C. Bank sees no economic ills over peso.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Manila C. Bank sees no economic ills over peso.

text.p: The sharp depreciation of the Philippine peso against the U.S. dollar should not hurt the growing domestic economy, Central Bank governor Gabriel Singson said on Friday.

A weaker peso would help improve the dwindling fiscal surplus of the government, while the prevailing low inflationary regime and debt servicing ratio could easily weather the short-term adjustments it brings, Singson told a news conference shortly after the bank announced it would allow the peso to trade in a wider range.

The move meant an effective devaluation of the currency and the peso plunged 11.5 percent to 29.45 per dollar before trades were finally suspended by the Bankers Association of the Philippines. This is the lowest level since September 1993.

In the past 10 days, the Philippine peso had been under tremendous pressure and the Central Bank had defended it by selling over $1 billion and raising its overnight interest rate to a 2 1/2-year high of 32 percent.

Singson denied there was political pressure for the Central Bank to stop defending the peso and said the decision to allow the peso to weaken was taken in order to protect the country's foreign exchange reserves.
Latest figures show reserves have fallen by $2.5 billion to just $10 billion since March when the financial crisis in Thailand first began to spill over into the Philippine economy.
"It's very simple, we don't like to run down our reserves ... There's no political pressures ... We did not buckle down. We are adopting a different strategy against speculators," he said.
Though a weaker peso would raise inflation slightly in the short-term, inflation and interest rates will decline over a period of time and government revenues will improve, he said.

Filipino importers and foreign exchange borrowers are mostly exporters, and their foreign exchange risks are hedged, Singson said, as he debunked fears that a weak peso could lead to massive loan defaults.
Besides, he said, borrowers "have been more than compensated in the very positive interest differentials in their favour."
Dollar loans were being lent out at 7.5 percent, while the peso-denominated loans were being lent out at 14 percent, he said.
Singson said the fiscal situation could improve as a weaker peso would translate to higher customs collection.
A recent study made by the Department of Finance showed that a one peso depreciation would bring in an additional 4.0 billion pesos due to the higher landed cost.
This will help shore up the fiscal surplus which has been dwindling due to lower collection especially from the delay in the passage of a new tax law.
